sections.heading: What you have given me in Christ
sections.text: Father, God of grace, you have done what I could never do. You counted my sin against Christ, my substitute, and you counted his righteousness as mine. You have covered me with a righteousness that is not homemade and not earned. You have dressed me in the beauty of Christ, and you are making holiness real in me.
theological_themes: Substitutionary atonement: Christ bears the sinner’s guilt in the sinner’s place.
Imputed righteousness: God counts Christ’s righteousness to the believer by grace.
Salvation is received from God, not produced by human effort.
Holiness is both a gift of grace and a work God continues in the believer.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the great exchange at the heart of salvation: Christ is treated as sin for us so that we may become righteous in him. This directly grounds the prayer’s confidence that sin is laid on the substitute and righteousness is given to the believer.
Paul says God justifies the ungodly and counts righteousness apart from works. This supports the prayer’s refusal to bring its own righteousness and its reliance on God’s gracious accounting.
Isaiah uses the imagery of being clothed with garments of salvation and a robe of righteousness. That image helps express the prayer’s language of being covered by a righteousness God provides.

sections.heading: Seeing how sin still clings to me
sections.text: And yet, Lord, when I look honestly at my daily life, I still see how deeply sin is tangled up in me. Even my best prayers need mercy. My sorrow over sin is not as clean as I wish it were. My confessions can still be mixed with pride, self-protection, and excuses. Even when I receive your gifts, I can turn them toward myself. I do not want to pretend that my spiritual life is purer than it is.
theological_themes: Remaining sin continues to affect the believer’s motives, words, and worship.
Self-examination before God exposes mixed motives and spiritual pride.
Even sincere religious acts need the cleansing mercy of God.

scripture_references.connection: Isaiah confesses that even what appears righteous among God’s people is polluted when measured by God’s holiness. This supports the prayer’s honest admission that its best acts are not free from sin.

Paul describes the painful conflict between the renewed desire to obey God and the continuing presence of sin. This gives biblical shape to the prayer’s grief over sin that remains within the Christian life.

sections.heading: Bringing even my repentance to be cleansed
sections.text: So I come to you with nothing to boast in, not even my repentance. I need to repent of the way I repent. I need my tears washed too. I have no robe of my own to bring you and no way to manufacture a righteousness that could cover me. Left to myself, I stand exposed and unclean. But by grace you keep clothing me again. You justify the ungodly. You welcome me when I have wandered far away. Again and again I come home saying, “Father, forgive me,” and again and again you meet me with mercy and cover my shame.
theological_themes: Repentance itself does not earn forgiveness; it must rest on grace.
God justifies sinners who have no righteousness of their own.
The Father welcomes repentant prodigals with mercy rather than rejection.
Forgiveness is grounded in God’s grace, not in the quality of the believer’s sorrow.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus’ parable shows the father receiving the returning son with compassion and clothing him with the best robe. This undergirds the prayer’s picture of continually returning home as a prodigal to a merciful Father.

Joshua the high priest stands in filthy garments, and God commands that they be removed and replaced with clean clothes. This passage closely supports the prayer’s image of God graciously changing the sinner’s garments.
John calls believers to honest confession rather than denial, with confidence that God forgives and cleanses. This grounds the prayer’s repeated return to God for mercy and purification.

sections.heading: Wearing Christ’s righteousness through all of life
sections.text: Let me live every part of my life covered by Christ. Let me begin each morning in him and come back each evening in him. Let me go into ordinary work wearing his righteousness, not my own. Let me enter every calling, every joy, every sorrow, and even death itself in him. When I stand before you at the last judgment, let me stand only in Christ. And when you bring me into your kingdom, let me shine with the glory you have given, not because I earned it, but because grace has brought me all the way home.
theological_themes: The believer’s whole life is lived in dependence on Christ’s righteousness.
Union with Christ gives confidence in daily life, death, judgment, and glory.
Final hope rests on grace from beginning to end.

scripture_references.connection: Paul rejects a righteousness of his own and seeks to be found in Christ with the righteousness that comes through faith. This supports the prayer’s desire to live and die clothed only in Christ.
Paul declares that those who are in Christ are not under condemnation. This grounds the prayer’s confidence about standing before God in Christ rather than in personal merit.
The redeemed are pictured as clothed in robes made clean through the Lamb, and they are brought safely into God’s presence. This illuminates the prayer’s hope of entering heaven clothed by grace.

sections.heading: Keeping the wonder clear in my heart
sections.text: Please do not let me grow dull to what is true. Keep showing me how serious sin is, so I do not make peace with it. Keep showing me how complete your salvation is, so I do not try to add to it. Keep showing me the greatness and beauty of Christ. Keep making holiness lovely to me, not just necessary. And keep me amazed that grace is still grace: undeserved, overflowing, and enough for me.
theological_themes: Sin must be seen truthfully in its seriousness before God.
Christ’s salvation is complete and sufficient.
Holiness is beautiful because it reflects God and is formed by grace.
Grace remains astonishing because it is undeserved and effective.

scripture_references.connection: Paul explains that the law exposes sin as truly sinful. This supports the prayer’s request not to lose sight of the deep seriousness of sin.

Paul presents grace not only as pardon but as the power that trains believers in holiness while centering them on Christ’s redeeming work. This connects the prayer’s wonder at grace with its longing for holy living.
Paul teaches that beholding the Lord’s glory is part of how believers are transformed. This supports the prayer’s desire to keep seeing the glory of Christ and the beauty of holiness.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original assumes a strongly Reformed account of salvation, especially substitutionary atonement and the imputation of Christ’s righteousness to the believer. These are historic Protestant doctrines, but they are articulated differently or contested in some Christian traditions.

The phrase “I need to repent of my repentance” could be misunderstood as morbid self-condemnation. It has been preserved in sense as a confession that even sincere repentance is imperfect and must rest on grace, not as a denial that repentance is a real gift of God.

The reference to standing before the “great white throne” draws from final judgment imagery. Because Revelation 20’s great white throne scene is interpreted differently among Christians, the adaptation renders it more generally as standing before God at the last judgment while preserving the original’s seriousness.
significant_interpretive_choices: The original’s images of robes, rags, and changed clothing were retained because they carry the prayer’s core meaning: the believer has no adequate righteousness of their own and must be clothed by God in Christ.

The line about “receiving the Spirit” being mixed with selfishness was rendered as receiving God’s gifts and turning them toward oneself. This keeps the moral point without implying that the Holy Spirit himself is impure or diminished.

The repeated movement to the far country and back home was interpreted through the prodigal son in Luke 15, emphasizing continual repentance and the Father’s repeated mercy without suggesting that justification is repeatedly lost and regained.
